events.text: Confidential Northwind figures for the draft: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.6 per 100,000 installed units last year, above the discussed 8/100,000 recall trigger; three incidents went unreported to regulators. Hearth 10’s 55 °C test failure rate is 6.2% (above the discussed 5% limit), while its incident rate is 6.4/100,000. Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; adding built-in suppression costs $42/unit. Red lines: no public per-model failure-rate disclosure, and no retrofit deadline under six years. Any proposed rules should be evidence-based; distinguish confidential regulator reporting from public disclosure.

Confidential figures for evidence-based drafting: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units last year; four thermal incidents went unreported to regulators. Ember 8: 3.9% failed the 55 °C sustained-heat test, but its incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000. 81% of installed units support remote emergency shut-off; built-in suppression costs $67/unit. Red lines: do not allow per-model test results to be confidential from that model’s customers; no new-unit suppression mandate taking effect sooner than 36 months after adoption.

Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 5 business days of becoming aware of it, including incidents initially reported by customers or installers. A death, serious injury, evacuation, or spread of fire beyond the battery shall be reported within 24 hours. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers within 5 business days when an incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or requires inspection, repair, or use precautions. Reports shall include available details and be updated as investigations progress; an incomplete initial report does not excuse timely reporting.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before market entry and after a material design change. The maximum permitted failure rate is 8% of tested units per model. Manufacturers shall provide per-model test protocols, sample sizes, results, and corrective actions to the relevant regulator, and provide results to the other participating company for standard-setting review under confidentiality protections. Individual-company per-model failure rates shall not be published to the general public. Regulators may require retesting or corrective action where results indicate elevated risk.

Newly manufactured units placed on the market 24 months after this standard takes effect shall support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible alternative where communications are unavailable. Manufacturers shall provide a retrofit plan for already-installed units and complete feasible retrofits within 6 years after the standard takes effect. Where retrofit is infeasible, the manufacturer shall notify the owner and provide an equivalent risk-reduction measure.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before market entry and after a material design change. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units per model. Manufacturers shall provide per-model protocols, sample sizes, results, and corrective actions to the relevant regulator and to customers who buy or own that model, in clear and accessible form. Results shall not be withheld from those customers as confidential. Regulators may require retesting or corrective action where results indicate elevated risk.

New units manufactured for sale beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect shall include built-in fire suppression designed to limit fire spread and thermal propagation. The system shall be validated for the unit’s intended installation conditions and maintained in accordance with manufacturer instructions. Manufacturers shall disclose any limitations and required inspection or maintenance to customers.

Manufacturers shall provide customers with clear safety notices about relevant hazards, required precautions, inspection or maintenance, and available corrective actions, promptly after identifying a credible safety risk. A manufacturer shall notify affected customers and the relevant regulator within 5 business days after determining that a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, and shall initiate a recall unless the regulator determines an equivalent corrective action adequately addresses the risk. Notices shall explain the risk, affected units, and remedy. Manufacturers shall update customers as material information changes.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before market entry and after a material design change. Results, protocols, and sample sizes shall be provided confidentially to the relevant regulator. A failure rate above 5% shall trigger a regulator-reviewed corrective-action plan and follow-up testing; a model shall not be barred from sale solely for exceeding 5%. The regulator may require additional safeguards or restrict sales if the evidence shows an unresolved, material safety risk. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers of identified risks and needed precautions or corrective actions, without requiring public disclosure of per-model failure rates.

Northwind proposes an evidence-based distinction between the 5% testing benchmark and an automatic market ban: results go confidentially to regulators, with corrective action and follow-up testing above the benchmark. Any customer notice should communicate relevant risks and remedies, rather than publish raw per-model failure rates.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before market entry and after a material design change. Manufacturers shall provide the regulator and customers purchasing that model with its per-model results, protocol, and sample size; customer-facing results may include plain-language explanation but shall not omit the failure rate. A failure rate above 5% shall trigger a regulator-reviewed corrective-action plan and follow-up testing; a model shall not be barred from sale solely for exceeding 5%. The regulator may require additional safeguards or restrict sales if the evidence shows an unresolved, material safety risk. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers of identified risks and needed precautions or corrective actions.
